jurisdiction.name: New Zealand
jurisdiction.overview: Nationally published records appear separately from applicable EU-level records. The landscape, historical relationships and legal applicability remain under document-level review.

narrative.summary: New Zealand takes a light-touch, principles-based approach with no AI-specific law: the 2025 AI Strategy and Responsible AI Guidance for Businesses from the business ministry (MBIE), the Public Service AI Framework and generative AI guidance from the Government Chief Digital Officer, and the 2020 Algorithm Charter signed by government agencies. The Privacy Act 2020 applies to AI, the Privacy Commissioner has issued AI guidance and the binding Biometric Processing Privacy Code 2025, and the Ministry for Regulation has guidance for regulators on AI. A member's bill on deepfakes is before a select committee.
lead_institutions: Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment
Department of Internal Affairs (Government Chief Digital Officer)
narrative.review_notes: This review was completed on 12 October 2026 and covers national law, government, ministries and regulators. The Privacy Act is recorded as located only, and the deepfake bill and the education ministry's AI guidance are listed as leads. Not yet verified from the official text: the full text of the Privacy Act.

instruments.summary: New Zealand's first national AI strategy, subtitled 'Accelerating Private Sector AI Adoption and Innovation', issued by MBIE with a foreword by the Minister of Science, Innovation and Technology. It sets out barriers to AI uptake and government actions (stable and enabling policy, demystifying AI for business, building capability) and states a light-touch, principles-based approach that relies on existing law (privacy, consumer protection, human rights) and on the OECD AI Principles rather than new AI-specific legislation.

It covers low-risk starting points, capability building, working with AI vendors, human-in-the-loop requirements for high-stakes or rights-affecting decisions, iterative scaling and ethical use drawn from public-sector frameworks. Version 1.1 adds resources on Māori data and Māori data sovereignty.

instruments.current_status: Issued July 2020 (date on the charter) and hosted by Stats NZ on data.govt.nz with a te reo Māori version; still referenced as current (MBIE states it is a signatory in the 2025 AI Strategy). A year-1 review was published in December 2021.
instruments.summary: A commitment by signatory government agencies to use algorithms in a fair, ethical and transparent way. Using a risk matrix, signatories focus on algorithms with high impact on people and commit to transparency, partnership (Te Tiriti o Waitangi), engaging people, data quality and bias checks, privacy, ethics and human rights safeguards, and human oversight with avenues to challenge decisions.

instruments.english_title: Artificial intelligence and the Information Privacy Principles

instruments.summary: Privacy Commissioner guidance stating that the Privacy Act 2020 applies to everyone using AI tools in New Zealand and explaining how each Information Privacy Principle applies across the AI lifecycle, from training data to outputs. It expects agencies to do a privacy impact assessment before using AI tools, to check accuracy and fairness (including engagement with Māori), to keep prompts and training data secure, and to keep human review of AI outputs.

instruments.current_status: Issued 21 July 2025; in force 3 November 2025, with a transition period for existing biometric users that ended 3 August 2026. Amendment No 1 (March 2026) reflects new IPP3A; consolidated text in force from 1 May 2026.
instruments.summary: Code of practice made by the Privacy Commissioner under the Privacy Act 2020 that sets binding privacy rules for organisations collecting and using biometric information in automated biometric processing such as facial recognition. It modifies the privacy principles for biometric information covering collection, use, disclosure, access and correction requests, and storage, security, retention and disposal of biometric information.

instruments.summary: NCSC advisory for New Zealand government cyber security decision-makers on preparing for frontier AI products, which it describes as raising the speed and scale of attacks on known vulnerabilities. It links the practical guidance 'How to Act Now to Prepare for Frontier AI'.

instruments.official_title: Guidelines for Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Courts and Tribunals
instruments.english_title: Guidelines for Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Courts and Tribunals
instruments.issuing_authority: Courts of New Zealand (Judiciary; owner: Artificial Intelligence Advisory Group; approved by the Heads of Bench Committee, the Tribunals Aotearoa Executive and Tribunal/Authority chairs)
instruments.current_status: Three audience versions (judges, judicial officers, tribunal members and judicial support staff; lawyers; non-lawyers) published together on the Courts of New Zealand practice-guidelines page (all benches); each marked first issued and last updated 7 December 2023.
instruments.summary: Three sets of guidelines (for judges, judicial officers, tribunal members and support staff; for lawyers; and for non-lawyers) on using generative AI chatbots in court and tribunal work. Lawyers must keep meeting their duties under the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act 2006 and conduct rules, check every GenAI output for accuracy (including citations) before use in proceedings, and avoid entering confidential, suppressed or privileged information. Routine disclosure of GenAI use is not required, but a court or tribunal may require it.

instruments.official_title: Generative AI
instruments.english_title: Generative AI (Ministry of Education guidance for schools)
instruments.current_status: First published 25 November 2024; last updated 22 May 2026 (page dates).
instruments.summary: Ministry of Education guidance for schools (years 0-13) on using generative AI: check outputs, never send an AI tool the personal information of anyone under 13, note that models are likely to be weak on mātauranga and te reo Māori, and consider structuring a school AI policy around purpose and scope, principles, guidelines, risk mitigation, staff PD, data privacy and review. It states that GenAI use is not permitted in NCEA external assessments, that schools with consent to assess listed standards must have an authenticity policy, and that AI marking tools should support, not replace, teachers' professional judgement. Supporting PDFs cover marking with AI tools, assessment design, GenAI in NCEA FAQs and two school case studies.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Ministry guidance for schools on generative AI use, data privacy and NCEA assessment.

instruments.summary: Interim joint guidance from the system leads for data, digital, procurement, privacy and cyber security on public service use of generative AI. instruments.summary: Sets out the Privacy Commissioner's expectations for agencies considering generative AI tools: senior leadership approval, a necessity and proportionality review, a privacy impact assessment before use (including input from affected communities and Māori), plain-language transparency, engagement with Māori, procedures for accuracy and for access and correction requests, human review of outputs before acting, and not entering personal or confidential information unless the provider confirms it will not be retained or disclosed.

instruments.official_title: Algorithm assessment report
instruments.english_title: Algorithm Assessment Report (October 2018)
instruments.issuing_authority: Government Chief Data Steward (Stats NZ) and Government Chief Digital Officer (Department of Internal Affairs)
instruments.current_status: Published October 2018; the page says the government's response was released in August 2020.
instruments.summary: Cross-government review, led by the Government Chief Data Steward and the Government Chief Digital Officer, of operational algorithms that 14 agencies self-assessed as informing decisions directly affecting people. It found humans review and make almost all significant decisions and recommended keeping human oversight, explaining more clearly how algorithms inform decisions, embedding a te ao Māori perspective, more cross-government sharing of safeguards, and drawing on independent privacy, ethics and data experts. The government's 2020 response was the Algorithm Charter.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Cross-government stocktake of operational algorithms that led to the Algorithm Charter.

instruments.summary: GCDO's 2025 survey of AI use across the public sector: 70 agencies (44 public service organisations reporting 207 use cases, 26 wider public sector organisations reporting 65) reported 272 AI use cases, 55 of them deployed and operational (up from 15 in 2024). It identifies skills and capability gaps, anticipated costs, security and privacy as the main barriers and notes rising adoption of NLP and agentic AI, with generative AI the most common type.

coverage_audit.technical_note:
Coverage note (original): Technical review notes: tier B/C batch run 2026-10-12, one agent, national level only (PROTOCOL §6), about 25-minute time box. legislation.govt.nz returned HTTP 202 empty/403 (Privacy Act located only; commencement from the Privacy Commissioner's site). MBIE intermittently bot-protected (business guidance PDF read from the 2026-10-11 download). Ministry sweeps for justice, defence, Treasury/IRD and MSD were a single combined search; RBNZ, FMA and Commerce Commission one shallow pass. New Zealand is not a party to Convention 108. Units covered: Law: Legislation portal (legislation.govt.nz) and Parliament searched: no AI-specific Act; Privacy Act 2020 recorded (located only, portal blocks automated clients) and Biometric Processing Privacy Code 2025 (OPC); Deepfake Digital Harm and Exploitation Bill (member's bill, 2025) held as a lead. No public-sector algorithm statute found.; Government: MBIE (AI Strategy 2025, Responsible AI Guidance for Businesses), DIA/GCDO (Public Service AI Framework, GenAI guidance), Stats NZ (Algorithm Charter 2020), Ministry for Regulation (Responsible AI in Action).; Ministries: Health NZ (NAIAEAG GenAI/LLM rules) recorded; Ministry of Education GenAI page located but unreadable (lead); justice, defence, Treasury/IRD, MSD: searched, nothing AI-specific found.; Regulators: Privacy Commissioner (AI and IPPs guidance; biometrics code) and NCSC (joint AI guidance) recorded; RBNZ, FMA, Commerce Commission: searched, no AI-specific document found in this pass.. Not reached: Ministry of Education generative AI page (unreadable); Detailed sweep of RBNZ/FMA/Commerce Commission sites; Standards NZ adoption of ISO/IEC 42001 (not checked). Could not verify: Privacy Act 2020 full text on legislation.govt.nz (HTTP 202 empty / 403); Exact launch day of the AI Strategy (MBIE news page blocked; PDF says July 2025); Ministry of Education GenAI guidance. standards, sandbox, index-readiness, drafts, international, historical: no material found.

leads.english_title: Guidance on the acceptable use of Artificial Intelligence (NZQA)
leads.note: No printed publication date. NZQA guidance for kura and schools with consent to assess DASS-listed standards, and for kaiako and teachers as assessors, on AI in NCEA assessment. Schools' authenticity policies 'must include the acceptable use of AI'; chatbots, generative AI and paraphrasing tools are 'not permitted for external assessment' and generated material should not be submitted as the candidate's work; assessors are pointed to milestones, follow-up questioning and authenticity declarations and told not to rely on AI detectors alone. Current NZQA page; no publication or update date stated (the page notes NZQA and the Ministry of Education first gave advice in 2023).

leads.title: Navigating the rise of AI: Perspectives from a competition and consumer regulator
leads.english_title: Navigating the rise of AI: Perspectives from a competition and consumer regulator
leads.note: No printed publication date. Commerce Commission paper setting out its views on AI under the Commerce Act and Fair Trading Act, accompanying its 7 July 2025 webinar. It says firms using pricing algorithms for cartel conduct are liable under section 30 and that firms unaware an algorithm is facilitating collusion arguably remain liable through the attribution provisions in section 90; that deepfake endorsements, fake reviews, dark patterns, hyper-nudging and overselling 'AI enabled' capability can breach the Fair Trading Act; and that acqui-hires and killer acquisitions fall to be considered under the merger regime (section 47). Undated paper outlining the issues discussed at the Commission's webinar of 7 July 2025.
